archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (offense-led)
archetype.definition: A Texans team whose efficiency and even point differential belong to a winning club, but whose 2-4 start came from losing close games, bleeding hidden yardage and suddenly giving up explosive passes.

report.headline: A .500-caliber-or-better team wearing a 2-4 record; the bill for close losses is due.
report.take:
Houston is not a bad team that got lucky twice. It is roughly an average-to-good team that lost the coin flips. The Texans have scored 144 and allowed 143, their net EPA ranks 13th, and the point differential implies 3.4 wins, not two. That gap shows up as winsOverExpected of -1.35, 28th in the league, and a 0.25 win rate in one-score games. Losing 36-31 to Buffalo, 34-30 to Dallas and 19-17 at Indianapolis is the story of September. In none of them were they outclassed.

The identity has flipped from last season. In 2025 this was a defense-first, 12-win team: second in EPA allowed and second in points allowed, with an offense ranked 22nd. This year C.J. Stroud has started every game and the passing offense carries the team: 10th in offensive EPA, 11th in pass EPA, and a line that ranks 4th in QB hit rate allowed. The last two weeks were the best two passing games of the year, at Tennessee and at Jacksonville. The defense has dropped to 20th in EPA allowed, and the cause is specific. The front is still good: 18 sacks (3rd), a missed-tackle rate 4th-best, and explosive runs allowed 4th-lowest. The back end is giving up big plays, 30th in explosive pass rate and 27th in deep EPA allowed.

The noise around the record is mostly self-inflicted. Special teams sit 28th in EPA per game. They commit eight penalties a game, 24th in the league. They go for it on fourth down at the 29th-ranked rate. The run game can't stay on schedule: 3.3 yards a carry and run success 30th. None of that is random. The close-game record is the part most likely to swing back. Everything else is fixable, but it has to actually get fixed.

Where it heads depends on the secondary and on health. Both starting safeties are on the report: Jalen Pitre is out, and Reed Blankenship is questionable with a concussion. That is the wrong unit to be thin in, given where the defense is leaking. Tank Dell is on track to debut, which adds another target to a passing game already working. With a division leader at 4-2 and the rest of the AFC South level with or below them, a 2-4 hole is very climbable.

strengths.title: Stroud's passing game is humming
strengths.body: The offense ranks 10th in EPA and 11th in pass EPA. The protection is clean enough, 4th in QB hit rate allowed, for Stroud to work the full field. The last two weeks produced pass EPA of 10.5 and 13.9, the best stretch of the year. It is spread across a tight end, several receivers and Nico Collins, so it isn't fragile to one injury. Dell's return adds depth.

strengths.title: Front seven still wins up front
strengths.body: The pass rush has 18 sacks, 3rd in the league. The run defense rarely breaks, 4th in explosive rush rate allowed, and tacklers finish, with the 4th-best missed-tackle rate. That is the carryover from last year's elite unit, and it is the kind of strength that holds up week to week.

strengths.title: Point differential says winning team
strengths.body: Six games of even scoring and a 13th-ranked net EPA point to a team that should be around .500 or better. The difference is close-game variance. History says Houston is usually on the right side of it: it ranked 4th in one-score win rate in 2023 and posted positive winsOverExpected in each of the last three seasons.

concerns.title: Secondary giving up the big ones
concerns.body: The defense is 30th in explosive pass rate allowed and 27th in deep EPA. That is the core reason it fell from 2nd in EPA allowed last year to 20th now. Both starting safeties are currently on the injury report, so the problem could get worse before it gets better.

concerns.title: A run game that can't stay ahead
concerns.body: The Texans average 3.3 yards a carry, 28th, and their run success rate is 30th. That leaves Stroud in too many long down-and-distance spots. The line's 20th-ranked yards before contact says the blocking is part of it, not just the backs. David Montgomery is out, so Woody Marks carries the load.

concerns.title: Hidden yardage losing close games
concerns.body: Special teams rank 28th in EPA per game. Penalties run at eight a game, 24th, and the team has 428 penalty yards. In a season decided by a handful of points, that is likely the difference in at least one of the losses. It is controllable, but it has been consistent.

trend.note: After a Week 2 dud against Cincinnati and three losses in September, the passing offense has taken off. It produced two straight wins with pass EPA above 10, including a road win at division-leading Jacksonville as an underdog.

nextGame.headline: Clean pocket for Stroud against a Giants team overachieving its play
nextGame.body:
The Book has Houston -10 with a total of 42.5, and on paper the matchup leans their way. The Giants are 3-2-1 but have been outscored, and their winsOverExpected of 0.94 suggests the record is ahead of the play. Their defense generates almost no pressure: 30th in pressure rate and 31st in QB hit rate. That is a gift for an offense whose protection is already sound. The catch is where New York is good: it ranks 2nd in deep EPA allowed, holds tight ends down (5th against TE1 production), and runs a ball-control offense that ranks 3rd in time of possession. Expect Houston to win short and intermediate rather than over the top, and to face a team that tries to shorten the game.

Availability cuts both ways. Houston is without safety Jalen Pitre, and Reed Blankenship is questionable with a concussion, which thins the deep middle exactly where the defense has struggled. Montgomery is out, so Marks is the lead back, and Tank Dell is expected to make his season debut. The Giants are banged up too. Right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor, safety Tyler Nubin, corner Colton Hood and tight end Theo Johnson are out, while linebacker Tremaine Edmunds, corner Greg Newsome II and receiver Darnell Mooney are questionable. Jameis Winston has started the last four games at quarterback.

waysToWin.title: Stroud dissects a non-existent pass rush
waysToWin.body: New York ranks 30th in pressure rate and 30th in sack rate. Stroud should have time to work the middle of the field to his receivers. Because the Giants defend the deep ball well, the edge is volume and efficiency underneath, not shot plays.

waysToWin.title: Pass rush feasts on short-handed line
waysToWin.body: The Giants allow sacks at the 25th-ranked rate and are now without their starting right tackle. Houston's defense ranks 9th in sack rate. Forcing Winston into long yardage takes away the run-first, clock-eating script New York prefers.

waysToWin.title: Marks finds explosive runs
waysToWin.body: The Giants are 29th in explosive rush rate allowed and have let lead backs beat their averages, 29th against RB1. This is the week Houston's sputtering ground game can break a few chunks and finally stay on schedule.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers and special teams swing it
waysToLose.body: New York ranks 7th in takeaways and 7th in special teams EPA, while Houston is 28th on special teams. A short field or two plus a return can turn a talent gap into a one-score game. One-score games are exactly where the Texans have stumbled.

waysToLose.title: Giants shrink the game
waysToLose.body: New York runs far more than expected and ranks 3rd in time of possession. Fewer possessions make a 10-point spread hard to reach and keep an underdog alive late. If Houston's run game stalls again, it cannot answer by controlling the clock itself.

waysToLose.title: Deep shots against backup safeties
waysToLose.body: Houston's secondary already ranks 27th in deep EPA allowed. With Pitre out and Blankenship questionable, Winston will test it. A couple of busted coverages is the quickest way this becomes a loss.

nextGame.watch: Whether Houston's patched-together safety group can keep Winston from hitting the explosive passes that have defined its defensive slide.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency profile points to a team that wins more than it loses from here. The close-game luck should even out, the passing offense is trending up, and Dell adds a weapon. The schedule has winnable stretches: a winless Chargers team, Indianapolis, Washington, Philadelphia and Tennessee. It also has a stiff run through Baltimore, Pittsburgh, Jacksonville and Green Bay. With the AFC South leader only two games clear, a playoff push is realistic. That is especially true with home division games against Jacksonville and Tennessee still ahead.

What's sustainable: Stroud's passing efficiency, the pass rush and the run defense. What should regress toward the team's norms: the one-score losing and some of the penalty volume. What probably doesn't fix itself: the run game, given the line's yards-before-contact numbers. The deep-ball defense is the true swing. Last year's unit was elite, so a healthy secondary could pull it back toward the middle. A long absence for both safeties would keep the Texans in shootouts they have struggled to close.
swingFactors: Safety health and the deep-pass defense
Close-game and special-teams variance evening out
Whether the run game can stay on schedule

confidence.note: Six games, a defensive profile far from last season's, and key safeties hurt.
